newsitem.title: USA: Embassy takeover spotlights imprisoned U.S. woman.
newsitem.headline: Embassy takeover spotlights imprisoned U.S. woman.

text.p: Locked in a Peruvian cell 23-1/2 hours a day, her fingers swollen purple from the thin highland air, Lori Berenson has unwittingly sprung back into prominence following the rebel seizure of the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.
Shots of the 27-year-old New Yorker, splashed in U.S. papers and on network TV, have re-trained the spotlight on the American woman sentenced to life without parole last January.
Berenson was convicted by a secret military tribunal of involvement with the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), the force holding about 340 hostages since Tuesday.
U.S. media highlighted her rebel connection, despite her protests of innocence and demand for a civilian trial.
Berenson has expressed sympathy for the MRTA, but rejects charges of participation in guerrilla activity.
The MRTA is demanding freedom for all its imprisoned members, but so far it has not cited her name in petitions.

A "faceless" military tribunal convicted her on accusations said to have included transporting arms and renting a Lima house as an MRTA front. Another charge was intelligence gathering for an alleged rebel plot for a spectacular takeover of congress.
Berenson has long sought to demonstrate her innocence in civilian court by producing evidence and having a lawyer confront witnesses, her mother Rhoda Berenson told Reuters this week.
Backing the demand for an open trial are President Bill Clinton, 107 members of Congress, the U.S. State Department and former President Jimmy Carter.
When her parents visited her on December 7 at a remote jail, they brought a dozen of her favourite New York bagels, chocolate chip cookies and other treats as well as medicine.
But Mrs. Berenson said the meeting was "extremely tense."
"More than anything else, Lori wanted to know what prospects there were for a civilian trial," Mrs. Berenson said of their first meeting with her in a year.
Contributing to the strain was the fact time was short -- only 30 minutes, the maximum allowed by Peruvian authorities.
Now that Lori has been behind bars for a year, Peru is allowing one family visit monthly to her in Yanamayo, 530 miles (850 km) southeast of Lima and 13,000 feet (3,962 metres) above sea level.

Due to the altitude, Lori's fingers have swollen and turned purple, making writing painful, Mrs Berenson said. "It's a natural reaction of lowlanders," she explained. "They have to produce a lot of extra red-cells and thicken capillaries to get more oxygen."
Other highland-related ailments were dizzy spells, cut fingers and inability to digest beans and herbs.
A sore throat and laryngitis were chronic due to confinement in an unheated cell 23-1/2 hours a day, Mrs. Berenson added.
U.S. and Peruvian sources confirmed the lock-in schedule in Yanamayo, where temperatures often plunge below freezing.
Despite Lori's hardship, her parents draw encouragement from the widening support for a new trial.
In early August, a bipartisan group of 20 U.S. senators and 87 U.S. representatives sent strong letters to Fujimori.
Their letters attack Peru's military tribunals where judges are known as "faceless" since they wear hoods and operate behind closed doors.
The representatives asked Fujimori to free Berenson, set aside the military convictions or provide a fair, public trial. In a briefer letter, the senators demanded a civilian trial.
Fujimori has not responded to either letter, the Berensons and their U.S. Congress representative, New York Democrat Carolyn Maloney, said.
One psychological boost for the Berensons came when Clinton raised the case with Fujimori in a May 21 White House meeting.

Clinton asked for a review of the due process issue, White House spokeman David Johnson said after the meeting. Separately, Press Secretary Mike McCurry said Lori Berenson was entitled to due process in a Peruvian civilian court.
Fujimori said the president made no request on the case, but he confirmed that he discussed Berenson with Clinton.
In late August, House of Representatives Deputy Whip Representative Bill Richardson raised the Berenson case with Fujimori in Lima, his spokesman said.

One sign of widening interest is a surge of visits to an Internet Web site devoted to Berenson. On Friday, the site had 377 "hits" in a 15-3/4-hour period, over four times the normal traffic, Mark Berenson told Reuters.
